Seventy-seven seasons.
One connected pit wall.

A blog research pack about the data, engineering and prediction record behind F1nsight, with real product screenshots and reusable figures.

01 / the scale

A small site with a long memory

77seasons represented, 1950–2026
1,166races with recorded results
635,331lap-time rows
881driver catalog records
12,881pit-stop records
326exported telemetry sessions

The database also holds 214 constructor and 78 circuit records, 26,247 race-result rows and 1,172 scheduled race records. Those six scheduled races without results are not counted as completed races.

02 / the engineering

Build once, serve static files

Python ingestion normalizes several public feeds into Parquet and SQLite. The modelling layer produces forecast and fantasy JSON. Next.js and React prerender the site, then Cloudflare Pages serves the static export. The live timing relay is a separate FastAPI and WebSocket service.

01 / CollectJolpica, F1DB, FastF1, OpenF1, FIA, fantasy feeds
02 / NormalizePython, Parquet, canonical IDs, SQLite, compact telemetry JSON
03 / ForecastXGBoost + set transformer + retirements + Monte Carlo
04 / PublishNext.js static export → Cloudflare Pages; separate live relay

GitHub Actions performs refreshes and retraining. A Cloudflare cron Worker dispatches checks, with GitHub schedules as a backup. Data persists in versioned GitHub release assets; refresh and retraining write separate groups. A promotion gate compares a candidate with the published backtest before replacing the model.

The standard forecast requests 20,000 Monte Carlo simulations. That is a sampling budget, not an accuracy guarantee. The current serving path is verified in site/next.config.ts; older overview prose in the README describes an earlier request-time rendering design.

03 / the record

Better forecasts, without pretending F1 is predictable

The published test covers 65 races: 24 in 2024, 24 in 2025 and 17 in 2026. It uses a walk-forward setup, training on earlier races and refreshing the model every three rounds. These are retrospective out-of-sample tests, not 65 forecasts logged live before the races.

The claim worth publishing: After qualifying, the model ranks the field slightly better than the grid and gives the eventual winner better probabilities on average. It does not beat the grid on every metric.
MethodWinner ↑Podium slots ↑Spearman ↑MAE ↓Win log loss ↓
Model: pre-weekend27.7%56.4%0.6183.681.935
Model: post-practice33.8%59.0%0.6343.521.694
Model: post-qualifying55.4%68.2%0.7003.251.189
Grid baseline60.0%68.7%0.6803.221.533
Championship baseline30.8%57.4%0.6023.882.104
Recent-form baseline29.2%51.3%0.5694.10n/a

Spearman measures agreement with the finishing order. MAE is average position error. The grid baseline orders drivers by starting position, with win/podium probabilities learned from historical grid slots. The recent-form baseline has no probabilistic win log loss; “nan” means unavailable. Stage comparisons reflect different information available at prediction time.

04 / the sources

External information, with a clear job for each feed

SourceHow F1nsight uses itStatus
JolpicaRace results, standings, schedules, lap times and pit stops. The archive's historical backbone.Active
F1DBFills historical and session-result gaps; shared IDs are normalized before serving and training.Active
FastF1Session laps, sectors, tyres, telemetry and track positions. The site exports each driver's fastest lap.Active
OpenF1Historical laps, stints, pits, positions, overtakes and weather. Free historical API; live access has separate requirements.Active
FIA + race controlAnnounced grid penalties, with manual overrides. These alter the simulated starting grid.Active
F1 Fantasy + DHLPublic fantasy prices and points, plus pit-stop information. Some fantasy scoring components are reconstructed.Active
PolymarketWinner-market probabilities, when a usable event exists. Logarithmic pooling: 20% model weight before the weekend, 35% afterward.Live forecast
Open-MeteoObserved weather and timestamped forecasts are archived. Weather is not yet an active production prediction feature.Research
F1 live timingSignalR timing, race control and weather for the live service. Live car positions are estimated and labelled.Live service
A live forecast is not the core backtest. The current prediction path can pool model and market probabilities. The pre-weekend pool uses model exponent 0.20 and market exponent 0.80; later stages use 0.35 and 0.65. These are logarithmic pooling exponents, not linear shares. The 65-race charts above describe the core published backtest, not prospective proof of this live market blend.

FIA decisions supply concrete news such as penalties. General articles, rumours and team upgrade reports are not parsed into structured features. Market prices may reflect that information indirectly, but the site cannot attribute a price move to a particular news story. Weather is collected for research and is not yet an active predictive feature.

05 / the detail

From a result row to a lap you can inspect

The telemetry export contains 6,437 driver-session fastest-lap entries and 2,059,840 speed values. Each trace is resampled to 320 points. These counts describe the site's compact exports, not full-session raw sensor measurements or 6,437 unique drivers.

A missing Singapore export exposed a useful engineering failure: results were marked complete, while the derived telemetry file was absent. Cloud runners discarded the cache, so repeating an offline export could never heal it. The repair restores the four files and lets refreshes fetch missing telemetry from the past 14 days, even for sessions whose results already exist.

06 / what comes next

The next improvements should earn their place

  1. Log every live forecast before the sessionFreeze timestamps, input versions and model/market components. Score untouched future races separately from development backtests.
  2. Prove the value of market informationCompare model-only, market-only and pooled forecasts at identical lead times. Include liquidity, missing-market fallbacks and paired uncertainty estimates.
  3. Evaluate weather without future informationUse the timestamped forecast available before each race, not the weather that actually happened. Add it only if it improves a held-out test.
  4. Measure confidence and season driftAdd race-level bootstrap intervals, calibration checks and regime breakdowns. The existing seed tolerances estimate training noise, not full generalization uncertainty.
  5. Monitor the completeness of derived dataTrack expected versus exported sessions, stale predictions and source failures. A green workflow should not conceal a missing product feature.
  6. Explain fantasy approximation and live estimationEvaluate reconstructed scoring components separately. Keep estimated live positions distinct from recorded positions and expose freshness in the UI.
07 / publication notes

Use the numbers with their definitions attached

Snapshot date: 23 October 2026. Archive counts come from the cloud serving SQLite database downloaded for the Singapore repair. Telemetry counts include the repaired cloud payload, with all four Singapore endpoints and the live page independently verified. The published backtest was generated 13 October 2026 and ends at race 202617.

The counts measure product and dataset coverage. Visitor counts, pageviews, uptime, latency, Core Web Vitals and current hosting expenditure were not measured. “Free public sources” does not mean every dataset has the same license or that commercial redistribution is unrestricted.

Screenshots contain Formula 1 and team assets as displayed by the product. Retain source attribution and the project's non-affiliation notice when preparing the post.
